messages.author: 5f8b51633aa2f2a1
messages.subject: plot.ggplot
parts:
Would there be interest in defining

plot.ggplot <- print.ggplot

or would that lead to confusion? I know lattice does something like
this and it seems intuitive enough to me -- more so than telling folks
to print() -- but I can see that it might lead to some confusion with
base graphics.

Michael

messages.author: 065110cca96a6373
messages.subject: Re: plot.ggplot
parts:
Hi Michael,

I think you could, but I think typical show is more intuitive. For
example, suppose one saves a model object:

m <- lm(mpg ~ hp, data = mtcars)

to view it, simply:

m

people are used to this. ggplot2 works the same way:

p <- ggplot(mtcares, aes(hp, mpg)) + geom_point()

and to view:

p

no need to explicitly print(p) it. Again as with models, for a one
line save and view:

(p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, hp)) + geom_point())

is a standard approach. My $.02.

Cheers,

Josh

messages.author: 5f8b51633aa2f2a1
messages.subject: Re: plot.ggplot
parts:
Oh, I didn't mean to drop print.ggplot -- that's far too helpful in
interactive sessions -- I was thinking more of an alias intended for
folks who build up their graph over a few lines and then ask "and how
can I plot this?" I'd even implement it directly as an alias:

plot.ggplot<- function(x, ...) print.ggplot(x, ...)

No loss of back compatibility but perhaps just a little easier for
those just learning grid-based graphics who don't immediately realize
that print() methods are called automatically at top-level interactive
sessions.

I like the parentheses trick to trigger print() methods too, but I
think it's more of a (useful) cheat than a reasonable bit of design.

Incidentally, I first misread your email and found out that show()
also dispatches to print() on ggplot object

Best,

Michael Weylandt

messages.author: 065110cca96a6373
messages.subject: Re: plot.ggplot
parts:
My point is that print() used interactively is not needed at all.
Yes, () is a bit of a trick (although very common for books,
tutorials, etc.).

You can build up the plot over several lines, and then simply by
entering the name of the ggplot object, it will be show()n, which as
you point out, dispatches internally to print(). So my answer to "how
can I plot this" is the same for "how can I view any R object?" just
type the object name. Again:

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, hp))

p <- p + geom_point()

p <- p + stat_smooth()

p # final p shows which implicitly prints, how would: plot(p) be better?

non-interactive sessions where the object is not stored. That would
make more sense.

(incidentally the show an object works with Sweave and the new knitr
by Yihui Xie packages does just include ggplot2 graphics without any
printing like you were working interactively)

\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
<<fig=TRUE>>=
require(ggplot2)
